quote: You're using the word estimate, but the ad I responded to said that Tesla was looking for people that... The ad kinda inferred that there was no cost involved.
stewart_read: This is the customer directly checking the rep's language against a specific ad claim — a legitimacy test, not a generic cost objection. It also foreshadows the Tesla product-expectation gap that resurfaces at 03:11.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as a plain cost objection, but the customer's own framing ('the ad I responded to said') centers on truthfulness of the marketing, not price sensitivity.
coaching_implication: Manager should note the rep answered the cost half cleanly but never surfaced or got ahead of the underlying Tesla-branding confusion this ad is generating — worth flagging to whoever manages the ad creative too.

quote: I'll confirm because Thursday is Tuesday. Yes. There isn't any cost involved for, like, the installation. So there isn't any upfront cost, but that doesn't mean the equipment itself is free.
stewart_read: This is a direct, specific answer to a customer-raised condition-of-continuing question, not unprompted technical content — the customer asked, the rep answered. It reads as legitimacy repair in the moment, and it worked: the customer said 'Alright. Go ahead.' immediately after.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as setter_scope_creep (financial-mechanism explanation), but the content was responsive rather than volunteered, and the schema's escape hatch wasn't needed since the customer's question was gating whether the call would continue at all.
coaching_implication: This is a reasonable model for handling ad-based cost pushback — confirm what's true, clarify what's not, keep moving. Worth reinforcing as a good instinct.

quote: A lot of our customers really like it since, you know, you're not spending more than you are already. And if anything, you're spending less.
stewart_read: The rep asserts a savings outcome ('spending less') with no bill number on the table yet and no basis given — this is an ungrounded quantitative claim made before any qualification has happened.
coaching_implication: Flag this phrasing habit — claims about spending less should wait until there's an actual number to anchor to, or be framed as 'it's designed to' rather than an assured outcome.

quote: Yeah. The title itself is, we've got it in a trust with our daughter's name on it.
stewart_read: This surfaces a co-owner situation (daughter named on the trust/title) but the rep says only 'Okay. Great.' and moves straight to utility company — no follow-up on whether the daughter needs to be part of any future appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: The call disqualifies before an appointment is ever set, so this gap has no immediate consequence here — but it's a missed structural habit worth naming since the call never got far enough to test it.
coaching_implication: Minor note for the manager: when a title-holder other than the customer is named, the rep should register it for later even if the call doesn't reach booking, since the habit needs to be automatic by the time it matters.

quote: Well, you know, it varies greatly. It was almost, like, it was, like, $3.84 last month.
stewart_read: The customer gives a bill figure and the rep reacts ('Oh, jeez... I can definitely see why you're looking into this') but never flips it into a specific reason to move forward — the acknowledgment is warm but generic, and the call moves straight to the credit qualifier.
alternative_hypothesis: The number itself is oddly stated ($3.84, likely a transcription/rounding artifact for a much larger bill) which may have made a precise flip awkward — but the rep could still have flipped on the pain ('that's the kind of bill this program is built to bring down') without needing the exact figure.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to follow every bill reaction with a line that ties the number to the appointment's purpose, even when the number itself is unclear or oddly delivered.

quote: Sure. The ad showed that it was like Tesla, and these new panels look like shingles, actually. Or they weren't the ugly looking panels that sit on roofs. Are we still talking the same thing?
stewart_read: This is the specific, narrow version of the Tesla expectation gap the schema anticipates: the customer wants the Tesla shingle-style roof product, which Ion genuinely does not sell. The standard Tesla reframe (Ion panels + Powerwall + in-house roofing) would not resolve this particular ask, since the customer's want is aesthetic and product-specific, not a general confusion about who Ion is.
alternative_hypothesis: A rep could still test whether the customer would consider Ion's own panel product once the shingle expectation is corrected, rather than accepting the disqualification immediately — but there's no guarantee that would have changed the outcome given how specific the customer's want was.
coaching_implication: Don't expect a scripted save here — the honest answer is Ion doesn't have what he wants. Coach the rep to still ask one clarifying question ('would you be open to seeing what our panels look like before deciding?') rather than closing the door immediately after confirming the back-order status.

quote: Unfortunately, not. So those have been back ordered for the better half of this decade. We're probably not gonna see them for a minute just because nobody has them right now with them being so far back ordered.
stewart_read: The rep confirms the product gap honestly but makes no attempt to invert the moment — no redirect to the actual bill pain ($3.84/mo figure, however imprecise) or curiosity about the estimate itself before the customer disengages.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer's want was specifically aesthetic (shingle-style panels), an inversion attempt may not have worked — this is a case where the miss is real but the ceiling on recovery was already low.
coaching_implication: Even acknowledging the low odds, the rep gave up in the same breath as delivering the bad news. One more attempt tying back to the bill or the free estimate would have been a low-cost try before letting the customer walk.

quote: In that case, I'm probably not interested.
stewart_read: The rep accepts the disengagement immediately with 'No problem, Greg' rather than deploying the schema's curiosity-creation rebuttal for 'not interested' language.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the objection is rooted in a real product gap (Ion doesn't have shingle panels) rather than doubt about savings, the standard curiosity rebuttal ('most people tell me they're not interested until they see the numbers') may not have landed — but it was never attempted.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to at least try the standard soft-exit rebuttal once, even when the objection seems airtight — some customers will still take the free estimate despite the product disappointment.
